1.overview: After Joshua’s death, Judah and Simeon attack Canaanite towns, capture Jerusalem and several southern territories, and Caleb gives Acsah springs of water after Othniel captures Debir. The chapter recounts Bethel’s capture by Joseph’s descendants and lists the territories where Israel’s tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites, who remain among them or force some Israelites into the hill country.

sections.heading: Tribes leave Canaanites in the land

2.overview: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bochim for breaking the covenant and warns that the remaining Canaanite nations will become a snare; the people weep and offer sacrifices. After Joshua and his generation die, Israel turns to other gods, and the LORD describes a recurring pattern of oppression, deliverance through judges, renewed apostasy, and the nations left in the land as a test.

sections.heading: The Nations Left as a Test

3.overview: The nations remaining in Canaan test Israel, but the Israelites intermarry with them and worship their gods, leading to oppression by Cushan-rishathaim and deliverance through Othniel. After Israel again turns to evil, Ehud kills Eglon of Moab and leads Israel to victory, and Shamgar strikes down six hundred Philistines.

4.overview: After Israel again does evil, Jabin king of Canaan oppresses the Israelites for twenty years, and Deborah summons Barak to lead Naphtali and Zebulun against Sisera. The LORD routs Sisera’s army, Jael kills Sisera, and Israel grows stronger until it destroys Jabin.

5.overview: Deborah and Barak sing of the Lord’s march from Seir, Israel’s distress, Deborah’s rise, and the tribes that join or withhold support from the battle. The song recounts the defeat of Sisera’s forces at Kishon, Jael’s killing of Sisera, his mother’s waiting, and the land’s forty years of rest.

sections.heading: The Lord’s deliverance and Israel’s distress
Jael kills Sisera and Israel rests

6.overview: Midian and its allies devastate Israel, and a prophet recalls the LORD’s deliverance from Egypt and Israel’s disobedience. The angel of the LORD commissions Gideon at Ophrah, Gideon tears down Baal’s altar, and he gathers forces before testing God with a fleece.

sections.heading: Midian’s oppression and the prophet’s rebuke
Gideon gathers Israel and tests the sign

7.overview: The LORD reduces Gideon’s force to three hundred men so Israel cannot claim credit for victory, then strengthens Gideon through a Midianite’s dream and its interpretation. Gideon’s men rout the Midianite camp with horns, jars, and torches, and Israel pursues the fleeing army and captures its princes Oreb and Zeeb.

8.overview: Gideon appeases Ephraim, pursues and captures Midian’s kings Zebah and Zalmunna, then punishes Succoth and Penuel and kills the kings. He refuses Israel’s offer of dynastic rule but makes an ephod that becomes a snare; after his death, Israel turns to Baal-berith and neglects his household.

9.overview: Abimelech gains the support of Shechem, murders his brothers, and is made king; Jotham answers with a parable and pronounces a curse on Abimelech and Shechem. Conflict between Abimelech and Shechem escalates into the destruction of the city and the deaths of its leaders, while Abimelech is fatally struck at Thebez, fulfilling Jotham’s curse.

sections.heading: Abimelech and Shechem Turn Against Each Other

10.overview: Tola of Issachar and Jair of Gilead judge Israel in succession, and the account records their years of service and deaths. After Israel worships foreign gods, the LORD gives the people over to the Philistines and Ammonites, rejects their first plea before they abandon their idols, and Israel assembles at Mizpah as Gilead’s rulers seek a leader for the attack.

sections.heading: Israel’s Confession and the LORD’s Response

11.overview: Jephthah, expelled by his brothers, returns from Tob at the elders’ request and becomes Gilead’s leader, then argues to the Ammonite king that Israel’s possession of the disputed land is justified. The LORD gives Jephthah victory over Ammon, but Jephthah’s vow leads to his daughter’s death or lifelong dedication, and Israelite women commemorate her each year.

sections.heading: Jephthah’s Daughter and the Annual Mourning

12.overview: The men of Ephraim confront Jephthah over his battle with the Ammonites, and Jephthah’s forces defeat Ephraim and kill 42,000 men at the Jordan crossings using the word “Shibboleth” to identify them. After Jephthah’s death, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon judge Israel in succession and are buried in their respective towns.

sections.heading: Jephthah and Ephraim at the Jordan

13.overview: After Israel’s forty-year oppression by the Philistines, the angel of the LORD tells Manoah’s barren wife that she will bear a son, Samson, who will be a Nazirite from birth and begin Israel’s deliverance. The angel confirms the instructions to Manoah, ascends in the offering’s flame, and later the LORD blesses Samson as the Spirit begins to stir him near Zorah and Eshtaol.

sections.heading: The Angel Ascends in the Offering

14.overview: Samson insists on marrying a Philistine woman from Timnah, and the LORD uses the match as an occasion against the Philistines; on the way, Samson kills a lion and later finds honey in its carcass. At the wedding feast, Samson’s riddle leads to threats against his wife, its answer is disclosed to the Philistines, and Samson kills thirty men at Ashkelon to pay his wager before his wife is given to another man.

15.overview: After his wife’s father gives her to another man, Samson burns the Philistines’ crops, and the Philistines kill his wife and her father in retaliation. The men of Judah hand Samson over to the Philistines, but he breaks free, kills a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone, receives water from God at Lehi, and judges Israel for twenty years.

sections.heading: Samson’s Victory and Deliverance at Lehi

16.overview: Samson escapes the Philistines at Gaza, but Delilah learns that his strength is tied to his uncut hair and helps the Philistines capture him. After his hair begins to grow back, Samson brings down the temple of Dagon on himself and the Philistines, and his family buries him near Zorah and Eshtaol.

17.overview: Micah of the hill country of Ephraim returns the silver he stole from his mother, who uses part of it to make an idol; Micah establishes a shrine, makes religious objects, and appoints his son as priest. A Levite from Bethlehem comes to Micah’s house, accepts his offer of pay and provisions, and becomes his priest, while Micah expects the LORD to favor him.

18.overview: Because the Danites have not secured territory, five men from Zorah and Eshtaol scout Laish and report that its people live unsuspecting in a good, spacious land. Six hundred Danites take Micah’s idols and priest, conquer Laish and rename it Dan, then establish the idols and Jonathan’s priestly line there while the house of God remains at Shiloh.

sections.heading: The Danites take Micah’s idols and priest

19.overview: A Levite from Ephraim retrieves his concubine from Bethlehem after staying several days at her father’s house, then travels to Gibeah, where an old man offers them lodging. Men of Gibeah attack the house, the Levite sends his concubine outside and she is raped; after she dies, he cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel, prompting a call to deliberate and respond.

sections.heading: The assault and the concubine’s death

20.overview: Israel assembles at Mizpah, hears the Levite’s account of the crime at Gibeah, and demands that Benjamin surrender the offenders, but Benjamin refuses and prepares for battle. After two costly defeats, Israel sets an ambush, defeats Benjamin, pursues the survivors, and burns the Benjamite cities.

sections.heading: Israel assembles and hears the Levite

21.overview: Israel grieves that Benjamin may disappear and, bound by its oaths, takes women from Jabesh-gilead and later arranges for Benjamite men to seize wives at Shiloh. The Benjamites rebuild their cities and return to their inheritance, while Israel returns to its own, and the chapter concludes that everyone does what is right in his own eyes because there is no king.
